title: Older Adults Who Walk Like Someone 30 Years Younger Have Half the Risk of Cognitive Decline — Even With Alzheimer's Pathology
excerpt: A landmark study in Neurology identifies 'super movers' — people over 80 whose brisk gait appears to shield their brains from dementia, offering a deceptively simple biomarker that diaspora families can track as parents age
body:
A small but remarkable group of older adults appears to have found a biological shield against cognitive decline — and the secret is deceptively simple: they walk fast.

A study published in the July 2026 issue of *Neurology*, the journal of the American Academy of Neurology, has identified a rare phenotype the researchers call "super movers" — people aged 80 and older whose walking speed is at least 1.5 standard deviations above the average for their age and sex. In practical terms, they move at a pace typical of someone roughly 30 years younger.

Only about 6 to 10 per cent of adults over 80 qualify. But those who do appear to enjoy a striking cognitive advantage.

Half the Risk, Same Pathology

The study, led by Dr. Joe Verghese at the Renaissance School of Medicine at Stony Brook University, analysed nearly 4,000 adults across five international cohorts in the Health and Retirement Study network, the LonGenity Study, and the RUSH Memory and Aging Project.

The core finding: super movers had roughly half the risk of developing cognitive impairment compared to their peers (hazard ratio 0.49). They showed slower memory decline over years of follow-up and preserved hippocampal volume — the brain region most critical for forming new memories.

Perhaps most striking, when researchers examined brain tissue from participants in the RUSH cohort who had died, super movers showed similar levels of Alzheimer's-related pathology — amyloid plaques and tau tangles — as non-super movers. Yet they had been sharper and more functional during their lifetimes.

> ""This suggests they may possess resilience mechanisms that allow them to maintain cognitive function even in the presence of age-related brain changes," Dr."

"This suggests they may possess resilience mechanisms that allow them to maintain cognitive function even in the presence of age-related brain changes," Dr. Verghese said. "Understanding these resilience factors could help us develop new strategies to promote healthy brain aging."

A Biomarker Hiding in Plain Sight

Walking speed has long been called the "sixth vital sign" in geriatric medicine, and this study adds powerful evidence for why. Unlike expensive brain scans or blood-based biomarkers still in clinical development, gait speed can be measured with nothing more than a stopwatch and a corridor.

The finding also aligns with a growing body of evidence connecting mobility and brain health. A separate UK Biobank study of over 415,000 adults found that slow walking pace combined with the APOE-ε4 gene (the strongest genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's) was associated with a nearly fivefold increase in dementia risk — far worse than either factor alone.

45% of Dementia Is Preventable

The super movers research lands alongside a major review published this week in *The Lancet Healthy Longevity* by Curtin University researchers, which found that up to 45 per cent of dementia cases worldwide are linked to modifiable risk factors — physical inactivity, smoking, low education, social isolation, untreated hearing loss, and others.

But the review also delivered a sobering warning: simply telling people about these risks does not work.

"Awareness campaigns are important, but on their own they rarely lead to meaningful or lasting behaviour change," said Professor Mario Siervo of Curtin's School of Population Health. The most effective interventions, the review found, were community-based programs delivered through trusted local figures — peer educators, community health workers, and cultural leaders.

A companion study from the same Curtin group, tracking nearly 500,000 adults over a decade, found that sarcopenic obesity — the combination of low muscle strength and excess body fat — was independently linked to higher dementia risk. Crucially, obesity alone without muscle loss was not. The message: maintaining muscle matters as much as managing weight.

Meanwhile, research from the University of Minnesota School of Nursing has identified 14 specific modifiable risk factors for cognitive decline, six of which can be addressed through a single intervention — consistent physical exercise. Regular movement simultaneously tackles obesity, high blood pressure, high blood sugar, depression, high cholesterol, and physical inactivity.

Why This Matters for Diaspora Indians

For NRIs watching parents and grandparents age back in India — or ageing themselves in the US, UK, or Canada — these findings carry particular weight.

South Asians face elevated baseline risks for several of the conditions that accelerate cognitive decline: type 2 diabetes rates are roughly double those of white populations at the same BMI; cardiovascular disease strikes a decade earlier; and metabolic syndrome is prevalent even among vegetarians. Each of these is independently linked to faster brain aging.

The cultural fit is also significant. Morning and evening walks are already a deeply embedded practice in Indian households — from retired uncles circling neighbourhood parks at dawn to evening strolls that double as social time. The super movers study suggests that maintaining — and even pushing — walking speed, not just step count, could be one of the most consequential health investments an ageing person can make.

For diaspora families separated by oceans, gait speed is also something that can be observed during video calls or measured during visits. A parent or grandparent whose pace has visibly slowed may benefit from a conversation with their physician.

Sources: *Neurology* (American Academy of Neurology), July 2026; *The Lancet Healthy Longevity* (Curtin University review), July 2026; University of Minnesota School of Nursing; *Stony Brook University/Albert Einstein College of Medicine*
